title: Any agent anywhere: How to use Grafana Cloud with Claude, Cursor, and any other AI agent
description:
AI agents are becoming part of everyday engineering workflows, helping teams write code, troubleshoot issues, and automate tasks. But to be truly useful in production, these agents need access to more than code. They also need observability data and context to understand what's happening across your systems, investigate problems, and help you take action.At Grafana Labs, we believe that context should be available wherever you work. That’s one of the core ideas behind Grafana Cloud as the open agentic observability platform: the flexibility to work with your observability data through the AI agents you prefer—whether it’s Grafana Assistant, a coding agent in your IDE, or a tool you’ve built yourself—so you can investigate and troubleshoot issues without switching tools.In this post, we'll explore how to bring Grafana Cloud into your agentic workflows using tools like the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx, with practical examples along the way. You can also check out our ObservabilityCON 2026 talk in the video below to learn more.Three ways to use Grafana Cloud with AI agentsThere are multiple ways to bring Grafana Cloud observability data and context into your AI workflows, depending on where and how you prefer to work:Work directly in Grafana Cloud: Use Grafana Assistant, the AI-powered assistant built into Grafana Cloud, to investigate issues and interact with your observability data.Connect your preferred AI agent: Use the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring Grafana Cloud data into compatible tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Codex.Work with coding agents and scripts: Use gcx, the Grafana Cloud command-line tool, to give coding agents access to observability data directly from their working environment.Whether you're working directly in Grafana Cloud with Grafana Assistant or using your own AI agents, you can choose the approach that works best for you. Let's look at how the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx make that possible outside of Grafana Cloud.Investigate an alert from your phone with Claude and Grafana Cloud MCP serverImagine you're waiting in line at a coffee shop when a Slack message arrives from your director of engineering. Something is wrong with the frontend, and they need your help.Your laptop is still in your backpack, but you don't necessarily need it to start investigating. With Claude connected to the Grafana Cloud MCP server, you can pull out your phone and ask a simple question: "Why is the frontend slow? Is there anything firing?"Claude can use Grafana Cloud data to answer your question directly in the conversation. In this example, it confirms that an alert is firing, shows a chart of the relevant signal, and identifies which pages are affected.You can then ask a follow-up question: how is this affecting the health of the frontend, and what's causing the problem? Again, Claude can return a visual Grafana Cloud view directly in the conversation, giving you more context about the health of your frontend application and helping you determine where to investigate next.All of this happens without leaving the conversation or opening your laptop. By the time you get your coffee, you've already confirmed the issue and started exploring its impact.How it works: The Grafana Cloud MCP server and MCP AppsThis experience is powered by two capabilities: the Grafana Cloud MCP server and MCP Apps.The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI agents to connect to external tools and data sources. The Grafana Cloud MCP server makes your Grafana Cloud observability data available to compatible agents, allowing them to query alerts, dashboards, and telemetry to help answer questions and investigate issues.That means you can interact with Grafana Cloud data from the AI tools you already use, rather than rely exclusively on the assistant built into your observability platform.MCP Apps take this a step further by bringing interactive Grafana Cloud views directly into your AI conversations. Instead of returning only a text description of an issue, an agent can display relevant visualizations, such as firing alerts and frontend health, alongside the conversation.These views are delivered by the Grafana Cloud MCP server and can appear in MCP clients that support them.To learn more, see the Grafana Cloud MCP server documentation. Continue your investigation in Cursor with Grafana Cloud context and gcxNow imagine you've grabbed your coffee and opened your laptop. You want to take a closer look at the frontend performance issue and get some help from your coding agent.You navigate to Grafana Cloud Frontend Observability, where a dashboard shows elevated time to first byte (TTFB), one of the symptoms of the slowdown.You could manually copy the relevant queries, filters, and time range into your coding agent and explain what you're looking at. But Grafana Cloud provides a simpler way to hand off that context.From a panel on the dashboard, you can click a button that automatically gathers the relevant information, including the query, filters, and time range. Then you select your agent of choice—Cursor, in this example—and send the context directly to it.Now Cursor has the same starting context you were using in Grafana Cloud. Instead of explaining the issue from scratch, you can immediately ask it to compare the affected pods with healthy ones. Cursor uses gcx to query Grafana Cloud and begin investigating the differences.This lets you continue investigating in the environment where you're already working, with the relevant observability context carried over from Grafana Cloud.How it works: Give coding agents access to Grafana Cloud with gcxgcx is the Grafana Cloud command-line tool. It provides a way for developers and coding agents to interact with Grafana Cloud directly from a terminal. Because coding agents can execute shell commands, they can also use gcx to access observability data as part of their investigations.gcx includes curated agent skills that help coding agents understand how to use Grafana Cloud data for common tasks, without requiring step-by-step instructions. Agents can also discover available commands and use them to explore different parts of a system, including services, databases, and frontend sessions.For example, gcx provides commands to:Explore application services: Inspect services and their operations to understand application behavior.Investigate databases: List and inspect database instances as part of a performance investigation.Examine frontend activity: Access frontend application information and sessions to understand the end-user experience.Here's an example of available commands, with arguments omitted:gcx
├─ appo11y
│  ├─ services get
│  └─ services list-operations
├─ dbo11y
│  ├─ instances list
│  └─ instances get
└─ frontend
   ├─ apps list
   └─ sessions get
In our example, gcx gives Cursor a way to look beyond the original alert and query additional observability data to guide its investigation. And because gcx works from the command line, this approach isn't limited to Cursor. Other coding agents that can execute shell commands can use it too, making it possible to incorporate Grafana Cloud data into existing development and automation workflows.To learn more and get started, visit the gcx repository on GitHub.Bring it all together: Investigate issues in Slack with an open source agentWhat if you'd rather investigate an issue without leaving Slack? You can also connect an open source agent like Hermes to Grafana Cloud using both gcx and the Grafana Cloud MCP server.For example, imagine your team reports a drop in completed bank transfers, even though traffic looks normal. You can ask Hermes directly in Slack to investigate the issue, providing the affected application, time window, and relevant context.Hermes can then use gcx commands and MCP tools to investigate the underlying requests, examine user sessions, and compare the results with an earlier time window. From there, it can report its findings back in the Slack thread, with supporting Grafana Cloud links, potential causes, and recommended next steps.Wrapping upWith Grafana Cloud, you choose the agent, the model, the provider, and where you work. Grafana Cloud then gives your agent access to the observability context and tools it needs to help investigate issues, identify root causes, and take action.Ready to try it yourself? Here are three ways to get started:Start with Grafana Assistant to investigate and troubleshoot directly in Grafana Cloud.Connect your preferred agent through the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring observability data into compatible AI tools.Explore gcx to bring Grafana Cloud into your coding agents, scripts, and terminal-based workflows.

title: Only include resource detectors you need by building your own Collector
description:
There are many reasons for building your own OpenTelemetry Collector
distribution. The existing distributions are designed to be broadly useful,
which means they include many more components than what an individual deployment
uses. Building your own gives you the ability to select only the components you
care about, add your own custom components, and control exactly what ends up in
the binary you run in production.
One of the reasons I prefer to build my own distribution is to limit the size of
the binary I have to ship around and to ensure that the least amount of
dependencies are included. Fewer dependencies means a smaller binary, a smaller
attack surface, and fewer third-party modules to track when a vulnerability is
disclosed. The
OpenTelemetry Collector Builder (ocb) makes this
possible: you write a manifest file in YAML to select the components you care
about, and ocb compiles them into the resulting binary.

title: Siri AI dev preview 📱, ChatGPT races Google 📈, engineering is changing 👨‍💻
Bridging Alloy and OpenTelemetry: the OTel engine is now in Public Preview
description:
Many Grafana Cloud customers love what Alloy offers them, but we're also seeing a growing base of users who feel the same way about the OpenTelemetry Collector. We want to make it easy for customers to make the decision that makes the most sense, regardless of their preference.When we introduced the OpenTelemetry engine for Grafana Alloy, we set out to give teams a way to run native OTLP pipelines without giving up the power and flexibility Alloy is known for. Since then we've kept building: ironing out service installation support, enabling Fleet Management, and folding in feedback from early users. Today, as of Alloy v1.21.0, we're happy to share that the OTel engine has moved into Public Preview, running right alongside the default engine you already know. In this post, we'll dig into when you'd reach for each engine, walk through some of the most interesting use cases we've seen so far, and give a preview of where both engines are headed next.The motivation behind each engineBefore diving into specific new features, let’s recap why we have two engines in Alloy.Default engineThe default engine is a cross-ecosystem engine at its core; it's not tied to any single wire format or vendor. It can just as easily run a Prometheus pipeline, an OTLP pipeline, or a Loki pipeline, all defined using Alloy's own configuration syntax. That flexibility is what makes it a Swiss army knife: the same engine that scrapes Prometheus metrics can pull in logs over syslog for logs, ingest OTLP, scrape Prometheus metrics from embedded exporters, and route all of it to wherever it needs to go.OpenTelemetry engine There's a lot to like about being able to speak every ecosystem's language. But the telemetry landscape itself is moving in the opposite direction. Rather than translating between formats, the industry is increasingly converging on a single, shared model defined by the OpenTelemetry specification. That's what an OpenTelemetry Collector actually is: a pipeline that treats OTLP as the native format end-to-end, prioritizing portability and open standards over ecosystem-bridging translation. At its core, Alloy's OTel engine is Grafana Labs' own distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.Running the OTel engineIt's just a collector The OTel engine is an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution that ships inside Alloy. It runs standard collector YAML with no translation and no Alloy syntax. If you already have a collector config, you already have an OTel engine config.- otelcol --config=config.yaml
+ alloy otel --config=config.yamlThe rest of the CLI matches, too. validate, components, print-config, and --set all work the way they do upstream, so scripts and CI that call otelcol validate keep working.The same goes for the tools you deploy collectors with. On the upstream Helm chart, it's two values:image:
  repository: grafana/alloy
command:
  name: "bin/otelcol"The OpenTelemetry Operator used to fail on the Alloy image because it had no way to set the container command. We added spec.command upstream (Operator v0.153.0 and later), so now it's one line:spec:
  image: grafana/alloy:<ALLOY_VERSION>
  command: ["/bin/alloy", "otel"]For a non-containerized installation, the Alloy packages can run either engine as a service. Set ALLOY_OTEL_MODE=1 and the service runs the OTel engine against config.yaml. Read our docs for more information on how to set it up by platform.Fleet management Managing collector configuration by hand doesn't scale past a handful of hosts, so remote configuration was one of the first gaps we closed after the initial release. As of Alloy v1.19.0, you can manage OTel engine configuration centrally with Fleet Management. The OpAMP supervisor is embedded in the Alloy binary and runs through the new experimental otel-supervisor subcommand: point it at your Fleet Management endpoint and credentials with a supervisor configuration file, and Alloy handles the connection, pulls down your pipeline configuration, and applies changes as you publish them. See the Alloy otel-supervisor reference to get started.An escape hatch: the alloyengine extensionSometimes the component you need only exists in the default engine today. The alloyengine extension runs Alloy configuration inside the same collector process, so you can pick up that one piece without running a second agent.It's Experimental, and we expect it to stay that way. The two engines run side by side but can't pass data to each other directly, so anything that crosses over goes out over the network, usually OTLP.If you reach for it, tell us why. Open an issue on the Alloy repo with the component you needed. That list is how we decide which default engine pieces become native OpenTelemetry collector components next.Experiments with Grafana Cloud productsHeads up first: nothing in this section is supported, and you shouldn't run it in production. Part of what we're working out with the OTel engine is how Grafana Cloud's products behave when the pipeline is OTel end to end. Here's where two of them stand.Database Observability. Today the path that works is adding your existing Alloy config to the collector you already run. Your OTLP pipelines keep doing their thing, and the extension runs database observability next to them. The Database Observability app can't tell the difference:extensions:
  alloyengine:
    config:
      inline:
        content: |
          database_observability.postgres "default" {
            data_source_name = env("POSTGRES_DSN")
            forward_to       = [loki.write.grafana_cloud.receiver]
          }
          // ...the rest of your existing Alloy config

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: {}
      http: {}

service:
  extensions: [alloyengine]
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlp_http/grafana_cloud]A native collector path is in the works but still further off as we decide how to break the Alloy components out into OpenTelemetry native ones.Cloud Provider Observability. Alloy's cloud provider exporters, like prometheus.exporter.gcp, work through the extension the same way. The data will be identical when run in the alloyengine extension as when run in Alloy’s default engine. The more interesting result is what happens without Alloy’s native Prometheus exporters at all. We've been working with the Prometheus community to make exporters embeddable as libraries, so they run as real collector receivers instead of something a collector scrapes. With a collector built to include it, the GCP exporter is just another receiver:receivers:
  stackdriver_exporter:
    exporter_config:
      project_ids: ["<PROJECT_ID>"]
      metrics_prefixes: [compute.googleapis.com/instance]
      aggregate_deltas: true  # off by default; Alloy turns it onLooking beyond Cloud Provider Observability, the OpenTelemetry Collector Prometheus Distro is an official, experimental collector distribution that ships embeddable Prometheus exporters as OpenTelemetry receivers including blackbox, Postgres, Google Cloud Monitoring with stackdriver exporter and CloudWatch through yet-another-cloudwatch exporter. The receivers live in prometheus-opentelemetry-collector if you'd rather build your own with Open Telemetry Collector Builder (OCB). As they progress through the OpenTelemetry stability model we will look to add them to the OTel engine.Looking aheadOTel engine So what comes next for the OTel engine now that it's in Public Preview? Making sure you can properly debug your collector is high on the list. Support bundles are a key feature for this in the default engine —a single request to /-/support packages your configuration, logs, internal metrics, runtime flags, and pprof profiles into one file you can inspect before sharing. The OTel engine has no equivalent today, so we're building an OTel-native extension to match it. Stay tuned for more updates on that front!We also want to hear what's pulling you back to the default engine via the Alloy engine extension. The extension is there as an escape hatch, but we plan to break those pieces out into native collector components, the way we've started with Prometheus exporters. If you've reached for the extension, or held off on the OTel engine because something was missing, tell us what it was.Default engineThe default engine isn't standing still. Most of the work ahead is about one thing: making sure your data always arrives, even when something downstream is having a bad day.Prometheus: a better Remote Write Today  prometheus.remote_write is what keeps your metrics from disappearing when your backend goes down, and there’s a lot going on to improve it:Smaller footprint. Keeping what’s in memory and what’s on disk as small as possible to help in high scale environments and keep restart delays minimal.Pickup where you left off. Data that was in flight when Alloy restarted should still get sent.Remote Write 2.0. When we moved our own internal Prometheus workloads to it, egress costs for that telemetry dropped by more than half. You can try it in prometheus.remote_write today as an experimental feature, and we're helping push it toward stable upstream.Because prometheus.remote_write builds on upstream Prometheus, much of this work happens upstream, so it helps the whole Prometheus ecosystem, not just Alloy.Loki: pipelines that know when something failedAlloy's log pipelines still use a design inherited from Promtail, where components pass logs with no way to report back whether delivery worked. That's behind most of the rough edges you might have experienced: logs lost when Alloy shuts down, a slow stage holding up everything behind it, and file positions that advance before a line is actually sent. We're rebuilding the pipeline so success and failure flow back to the source:No silent gaps. A file's position only moves once its lines are delivered, and Alloy drains in-flight logs on shutdown instead of dropping them.Throughput that scales. A slow stage stops blocking the whole pipeline, so giving Alloy more CPU actually buys you more throughput.A WAL you can rely on. We're working through the known issues to take the loki.write WAL to general availability, so logs survive an outage or a restart on disk.Both engines are shaped by what we hear from the people running them, so tell us what you want us to focus on next. title: Trace linkage: connect the dots between your app traces and database queries
description: When an application request slows down, a trace can show a database call. Finding the database query behind it can be tedious, requiring you to switch between traces and database telemetry, as well as match timestamps or query text by hand. In Grafana Cloud, the Database Observability app already provides a window into all of your database telemetry, including query samples, performance history, and explain plan. But what if you could jump from that database call in the trace straight to its query details?OpenTelemetry database semantic conventions stabilized last year, giving us all a dependable shared language for describing database operations. That foundation has opened the door for what we call trace linkage, now Generally Available in Database Observability!What is trace linkage?With trace linkage, we try to provide a connection between OpenTelemetry-instrumented applications and database telemetry collected with Alloy. In other words, when you give us these previously-disjoint puzzle pieces, we’ll do our best to provide you as much supporting information between these two elements as we can. And we'll do it without making you tediously piece together timestamps and logs. From a database span in a trace, you’ll see a link on the query text. Clicking from there, the app searches for a connection between your database query and our opinionated view of your most relevant data in the Database Observability app. You can explore sampled query execution data or check out the query’s historical performance, alongside that query’s related schema and explain plan.This connection builds on the database attributes your OpenTelemetry instrumentation already emits. Grafana Cloud Traces, powered by Tempo, retain those attributes, and trace linkage uses the query text, database system, and database name to connect a database span to its supporting query context in Database Observability. We support the stable conventions like db.query.text and its legacy equivalent db.statement, so existing instrumentation can continue to benefit as teams adopt the stable conventions.How does it work?The initial idea for trace linkage came from this question: What shared context could connect application instrumentation with telemetry collected from the database?The answer was to leverage trace context: the trace ID and span ID. On one side we have an application trace with spans representing a query execution. On the Database Observability side, we are collecting telemetry from the database concerning query executions. As long as the telemetry we collect contains the same trace ID and span ID, we can make a link between the application trace and Database Observability. This led us to sqlcommenter, an open source project donated to the OpenTelemetry community. Its idea is (delightfully) simple: let the SQL statement carry a piece of trace context with it in a comment. With trace context propagation enabled, sqlcommenter injects the application’s trace ID and span ID into a comment at the end of the SQL statement. This is done at the level of an individual query execution, so this is like a shared thread that allows us to follow from a trace span to a specific query execution.We then search the trace ID and span ID in the logs that we generated in the Database Observability Alloy component: our component extracts traceparent from the SQL comment and includes it in query sample logs.Going beyond a traceparent matchHowever, having sqlcommenter enabled doesn’t guarantee that Alloy captured the particular SQL execution. That can depend on how short-lived a query may be or how often Alloy polls the database. Even if you are ready to use sqlcommenter, not every database engine is supported, and it can come with downsides for database caches. This means that you might have traces for which we can’t find a query sample in Database Observability, at least not with  sqlcommenter exclusively.We can go beyond sqlcommenter-based matching by using the query statement itself. When we can’t find an exact match, we look for matching query text in the telemetry collected by Alloy.That sounds straightforward, but the same query can look different on each side. OpenTelemetry instrumentation doesn’t always record statements in the same way: depending on the language and instrumentation used, literal values may be preserved or masked, and parameter placeholders can take different forms. Meanwhile, database engines apply their own normalization to the query text that Alloy collects. We account for these differences, along with formatting and comments, to find a match.Even when we can’t point you to the exact execution, you can still explore the samples and historical performance we’ve gathered for that query! This lets us make a meaningful link between your traces and Database Observability, even without sqlcommenter.Start with query text matching, then use sqlcommenter to match trace and span IDs exactlyTrace linkage can be a great tool for quickly connecting your database and application telemetry, so we're excited for you to try it today. If your application is already instrumented as an OpenTelemetry SDK that sends traces to Grafana Cloud and you’ve already set up Database Observability, then read our docs about setting up trace linkage to help you get started. If Database Observability has collected a query and the database span already includes its text in db.query.text or the legacy db.statement, chances are trace linkage can already match the span to that query without further application instrumentation.Once you’ve tried query text matching, you can optionally go beyond and match a trace to a specific query execution with the use of sqlcommenter, as this blog discussed extensively. This improves match precision; exact matches remain best-effort because Alloy may not sample that execution.And if you aren't sure where to start, ask Grafana Assistant for help, using natural language.

title: Instrumentation Hub in Grafana Cloud: start easier, stay in control
description: It's no secret that getting started with observability can be much harder than it should be. That's why, at ObservabilityCon 2025, we introduced Instrumentation Hub: a guided, scalable way to roll out observability coverage while still keeping you in control. Today, we’re excited to announce that Instrumentation Hub is now Generally Available in Grafana Cloud.As we hinted at before, this new iteration introduces selective OpenTelemetry SDK injection, giving you deeper runtime insights for a wide range of languages to complement eBPF instrumentation with a single click. What is the Instrumentation Hub?Instrumentation Hub makes the biggest bottleneck of starting with observability, instrumentation, faster and easier by leveraging open source eBPF and OTel injection.At Grafana Labs, we're champions of open-standards-based observability, but we also realize that getting meaningful coverage of your systems can often mean months of manual toil. Each layer requires its own instrumentation approach, balancing technology tradeoffs, and unique brittle steps. Organizational challenges exacerbate this process, making observability a moving target with uneven coverage, persistent blind spots, and ultimately leaving you wondering if the effort was worth the pain.We believe there’s a better way. Instrumentation Hub is a control plane for remote discovery and selective auto-instrumentation. It helps you go from zero to meaningful telemetry in a matter of minutes by removing the bottleneck of having to apply instrumentation by hand.How Instrumentation Hub worksThe premise is simple: you run a single Helm command on your Kubernetes cluster to install Alloy, our distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.Once installed, Instrumentation Hub automatically catalogs everything that’s running on the cluster, structured by namespace and technology. Teams can immediately see what exists, what’s instrumented, and what isn’t.Then, you use either the Grafana Cloud UI, an API automation, or your favorite LLM agent to describe what and how you want to collect and monitor.Under the hood, Instrumentation Hub translates these selections into observability pipelines without the need for manual configuration. Within minutes you can begin exploring insights across your infrastructure and services in the Grafana Cloud observability platform.And of course, this isn’t a one-time setup. Teams can come back any time and refine their observability scope by namespace and enable or disable specific signal collection to balance their observability budgets. Need profiles for a misbehaving service? Enable them temporarily. Too many logs from a noisy workload? Exclude them. Trying to reduce spend? Dial back collection where it’s no longer needed.Observability is a progressionLast year at ObservabilityCon, we introduced the idea of a hierarchy of observability needs as a mental model to chart an effective path for applying observability. We described how you should start from a bird’s eye view of your estate and gradually move towards deeper and more customized insights.Instrumentation Hub is built around this progression, facilitating observability in the right order for a maximum return on investment.At the base is the foundation everything depends on: infrastructure visibility, which provides insight into the machines the code runs on. Instrumentation Hub helps you get started at this layer by enabling Kubernetes Monitoring with the click of a button.Above infrastructure is baseline service visibility. RED metrics and service relationships provide a consistent, system-wide view so teams can quickly triage issues and narrow the search space before digging deeper. Instrumentation Hub populates Grafana Cloud's Knowledge Graph in a matter of minutes, providing rich context for humans and agents.At the next level, technology-specific and transaction-level insights become necessary. Distributed traces reveal application behavior across the full request path, exposing performance bottlenecks and dependencies that aren’t visible from the outside.This is where Instrumentation Hub stands out. It can selectively deploy OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation SDKs with the click of a button.Historically, this process meant installing a new Operator, deploying instrumentation CRDs, annotating your target applications, and restarting the pods. This work can span across multiple teams, ownership boundaries, or require a dedicated new collection layer. But now, the very same upstream SDKs can be rolled out to complement and enrich your existing baseline service visibility without any extra moving pieces and without disruptive restarts.Get started with Instrumentation Hub todayTry it out! The Instrumentation Hub is available to all Grafana Cloud stacks for your Kubernetes clusters running on Linux.If you’ve recently installed the Kubernetes Monitoring Helm chart you might be set up with it already. And if you're still unsure, ask Grafana Assistant for help!

title: Grafana 13.3 release: manage variables across dashboards, share findings with Notebooks, a UI refresh, and more
description: Grafana 13.3 is here, bringing more consistency and control to how you work across Grafana. Cross-dashboard variables help you manage shared dashboard controls from one place, while Notebooks let you capture and share findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. You'll also get a first look at Grafana's biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7, along with new ways to guide and refine dashboards built with Grafana Assistant.Below are just some of the highlights from this release. You can explore all of the updates in the changelog or our What's new in Grafana 13.3 documentation.Define a variable once and use it across dashboardsAvailable in public preview in all editions of GrafanaWhen multiple dashboards use the same variable, such as an environment, region, or cluster selector, managing it separately in each dashboard creates duplicate work and can lead to configuration drift. To address this, we’re rolling out cross-dashboard variables, which let you define a variable once and reuse it across dashboards in your Grafana organization.You can create and manage these variables from Dashboards > Variables, and scope each one as either:Global: available to every dashboard in the organizationFolder: available only to dashboards in the same folderWhen you edit a dashboard, add a variable from the sidebar and select Global or folder variable. Grafana shows only the variables available to that dashboard's scope, and you can add them one at a time or all at once. Viewers can still change the variable's value on the dashboard, while its configuration stays managed centrally, so shared controls stay consistent without editing every dashboard that uses them.To try cross-dashboard variables in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle. To learn more, refer to the cross-dashboard variables documentation.Consolidate and share your findings with NotebooksAvailable in public preview in all editions of GrafanaAn investigation rarely happens in one place. You might start on a dashboard panel, jump into Explore to run a query, and then ask Grafana Assistant what's going on. Until now, the evidence and your reasoning ended up scattered across tabs, screenshots, and chat threads.Notebooks let you capture findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. Add panels from dashboards or Explore, pull in findings from Grafana Assistant, and write your observations right next to the data. Teammates can then follow your investigation, understand how you reached your conclusions, and collaborate on next steps.You can use a notebook to:Explore a question about your data, keeping queries and notes side by side as your thinking develops.Document an investigation so the next person doesn't have to start from scratch.Prepare a post-incident review with the relevant panels already in place.You can create notebooks manually or with Grafana Assistant, then save and share them for future reference. The new Notebooks page also makes it easy to find and manage your work, with options to search, filter, edit, and export notebooks. Notebooks are gradually rolling out to Grafana Cloud. To try them in self-managed Grafana, enable the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle. To learn more, refer to the Notebooks documentation.A fresh new look for the Grafana UIAvailable in public preview in all editions of GrafanaWhether it’s adding new data sources or supporting new use cases, we’re constantly expanding what Grafana can do. And as AI-powered workflows with Grafana Assistant became a bigger part of how people use Grafana every day, we saw an opportunity to rethink how the platform looks and feels.With Grafana 13.3, we're introducing the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7. Built on an updated set of design principles, the refresh introduces new colors, typography, and UI components to create a more modern, consistent experience across Grafana.Updates include: New default dark and light themes. We've reworked every theme color, with more shades for flexibility, and main action buttons now have a solid, high-contrast style.Softer borders and floating components. Rounder corners offer a more modern feel, and subtle borders on cards, panels, and drawers create a clearer sense of depth. The toolbar and navigation also stand apart more clearly from page content.Updated inputs, drop-downs, buttons, and tags. We've resized our most-used components to be more proportional and consistent. Revised typography. A new type scale mixes font weights and sizes, rather than relying on size alone, so it's easier to see what matters most on a page. Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Your existing workflows and navigation stay the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins that use standard Grafana components and theme tokens will automatically pick up the new look, while those with custom styling can migrate on their own timeline.To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous design at any time, and we welcome your feedback as we continue rolling out improvements over the coming months.Build and edit dashboards with more control using Grafana Assistant Grafana Assistant can already help you build and edit dashboards from a plain-language description. Now, with Grafana 13.3, you have more control over that process, from reviewing and refining a dashboard plan before it's built to easily undoing changes afterward. Review a dashboard plan from AssistantAvailable in public preview in all editions of Grafana With dashboard plans, you can describe what you want to monitor, and instead of building it right away, Assistant proposes a plan in chat. The plan covers the dashboard title, tabs or rows, panels, visualization types, and variables, so you can catch a missing panel or the wrong chart type before anything is built.Select Preview to open a read-only version of the dashboard, then keep the conversation going to iterate from there. When the preview matches what you need, select Build it to generate the dashboard and save it.Quickly revert Assistant edits Generally available in all editions of Grafana Experimenting with different layouts and visualizations is easier when you can quickly undo changes you don’t want. With Grafana 13.3, you can now select Undo turn after Grafana Assistant edits your dashboard to restore it to its previous state. If Assistant changed multiple panels in a single request, you can undo all those changes at once.To learn more, refer to the Grafana Assistant dashboarding guide.More to explore in Grafana 13.3Beyond these highlights, Grafana 13.3 includes a range of updates related to data visualization, alerting, Git Sync, and more. For an in-depth list of all the new features, check out our Grafana documentation, the Grafana changelog, or our What's New documentation.Join the Grafana Labs communityWe invite you to engage with the Grafana Labs community forums. Share your experiences with the new features, discuss best practices, and explore creative ways to integrate these updates into your workflows. Your insights and use cases are invaluable in enriching the Grafana ecosystem.Upgrade to Grafana 13.3Download Grafana 13.3 today or experience all the latest features by signing up for Grafana Cloud, which offers an actually useful forever-free tier and plans for every use case. Sign up for a free Grafana Cloud account today. Our Grafana upgrade guide also provides step-by-step instructions for those looking to upgrade from an earlier version to ensure a smooth transition.Special thanks to our communityWe extend our heartfelt gratitude to the Grafana community! Your contributions, ranging from pull requests to valuable feedback, are crucial in continually enhancing Grafana. And your enthusiasm and dedication inspire us at Grafana Labs to persistently innovate and elevate the Grafana platform.

title: Bliki: LLM Voice
description:
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading
  the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common
  tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I
  do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference
  between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary
  of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather
  misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we
  are in an uncanny
  valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm
  reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM
  present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language
  changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language
  of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a
  new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard
  these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational
  difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit,
  don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I
  strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the
  LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel
  the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 
1
 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I
  have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that
  may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 
2

  Authors should fill the prose themselves. 

Say Your Writing is
  even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head
  and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice
  is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate
  regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies
  on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering
  to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the
  difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find
  writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing
  something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence.
  I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but
  the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As
  more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and
  comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An
  important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He
  finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's
  disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my
  old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't
  comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found
  LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who
  know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the
  smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native
  Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter
  to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 
3
. Maybe
  most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't
  have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my
  humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.


Notes


1: 
      Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know
      the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when
      I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a
      major periodical publication to clean it up.
    



2: 
      My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write
       should declare how they used it, usually in the
      acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that
      readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI
      for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for
      writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going
      to the source).
    



3: 
      Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't
      trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're
      communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the
      envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic
      organism.”
    




Acknowledgements

Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua
    Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on
    drafts of this post.

I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
description:
TL;DRGood developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production.
I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance?

The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is.

Building it right

Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right. It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right.

Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on.

Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet.

After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect.

And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own.

A week at the whiteboard

Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here.

What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day.

The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team.

When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story…

The application ran. The build was red.

The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it. If it’s red so often that people stop paying attention, how do we spot the next real failure? And if we can’t trust the checks, a green build stops being reassuring too. That’s exactly the uncertainty continuous integration was supposed to remove, and we’ve been advocating it for over 25 years.

We’re still working through how to address it. Remember this was an experiment to push the very edge of agentic development. Were too many agents working in parallel and stepping on each other’s changes? Was the system not yet modular enough for agents to work on separate parts? Or were changes simply arriving faster than the checks could finish? Or was it a combination of all of these and more? Either way we definitely need to rethink how we will solve the last mile challenges. I can see continuous delivery/DevOps as a movement having a resurgence and a rethink in the agentic era in the same way the rest of the development life cycle is being upended. And it isn’t just our experiment. DORA’s 2025 research found AI adoption is now linked to higher delivery throughput, but to lower delivery stability. Exactly what continuous delivery and DevOps were trying to solve for!

All of these challenges prompted some good arguments internally. What role should test-driven development play when you aren’t reading every line and the agent created the tests alongside the code? Where would acceptance tests, contract tests and checks at system boundaries give us more confidence without being too brittle? How much design should we do before setting an agent loose, given how quickly we can revise an approach? Is there an appropriate point we will know we have gone too far? One of the biggest puzzles in all this is the size of the batch. I have heard many teams are moving from Stories to Epics. Great for speed of development but can your CI pipeline handle that size unit of work at speed and in parallel?

The experiment team didn’t settle all of this in a week or even two (they ran it twice with different teams). I wouldn’t trust anyone who claimed they had. But this is exactly the kind of work I want experienced developers involved in: experimenting, questioning and helping us discover which practices hold up and where we need some new ones.

Off the groomed slopes

After coming away from this conversation with some of the senior developers involved I kept thinking about learning to ski. Kids will often head straight down the hill without fear, kind of like a new builder who has never put software into production and has never fixed an on-call issue at 3am (something I will never forget, right up there with every production issue I personally caused and the resultant learnings from those, which are burned in my brain forever). When I first tried to ski as an adult, I was thinking about what I might break. I wanted to ski, it looked so fun and freeing, but I was old enough to see the consequences and I didn’t fancy hobbling around London with a broken limb or worse. My biggest issue was I hadn’t yet learned how to turn or stop effectively and without that I was a runaway train on a ski slope.

When I shared a draft of this post with Martin, who also learned to ski late, he pointed out where the comparison breaks down (like all analogies I like to push them to the edge, pun intended). On a ski slope you’ve watched countless people reach the bottom with no broken bones. The instructors have taught thousands of people before you on the same slope. They know which skills matter and how to teach them. Agentic development right now is more like a backcountry trip across unknown territory. We don’t yet know which skills will matter most. Not many people, if any, have finished the trip safely and the feedback on how to navigate it is slow or non-existent. As Martin put it, we won’t know whether a heavily agent-built system works until it has run in production for a while, survived a few rounds of change, and not sent all our planes to Aberystwyth. Built is not the same as working in production. Or as Charity Majors puts it, “staging is just a glorified laptop. Only prod is prod”. Which is why when someone says “it works on my machine” it’s usually intended as a joke. Or at least I always laugh.

That solidified a nagging discomfort I have had with leaders, technical or non-technical, claiming devs aren’t curious, or are laggards slow to adopt, and putting that down to easy-to-point-at fears like missing writing code (I do too) and fearing for our jobs (who isn’t right now?). Our best developers aren’t nervous beginners on a nursery slope that everyone else has already mastered. They’re looking at unmarked terrain and asking sensible questions about the route. Telling them to be less cautious misses the point. They need to be on the team that maps it.

Of course, experience can also make us too attached to familiar practices. Some of what we learned on the groomed slopes won’t hold out there, and we need to be willing to test our assumptions.

A challenge for both sides

So there’s a challenge here for both leaders and developers. Leaders need to listen carefully enough to tell useful concerns from reluctance to change, and to create real room for experimentation. That means time, permission to get things wrong, and not judging success by how much code the agents produced. Developers need to bring their experience into those experiments and be prepared to find that some of their assumptions no longer hold.

Some familiar practices will become more important. Others will need a different shape. Nobody is going to hand us a map first.

If you care deeply about building the right thing and building it right, your judgment is exactly what this new way of working needs. Bring the caution. Then let’s set off into the snow.

title: Faster, smaller checkpoints: the File Log receiver now uses protobuf
description:
If you run the File Log receiver with a storage extension, the
Collector writes a checkpoint every time it polls your log files. That
checkpoint is how the receiver remembers where it stopped reading, so a restart
does not lose or duplicate logs. For years that checkpoint format was JSON.
Starting with OpenTelemetry Collector Contrib v0.164.0, checkpoints are always
written as protobuf. On our benchmarks, saving a checkpoint is almost 5 times
faster, loading one is more than 5 times faster, and the checkpoint itself is
about 35% smaller.

title: Evaluate AI models for observability: o11y-bench joins Fireworks' Specialized Intelligence Index and reaches v1.1
description: When evaluating AI models for observability, generating a plausible query or explanation isn't enough. Teams need to know whether an agent's conclusions are supported by telemetry, whether its changes to dashboards actually work, and whether it can deliver reliable results consistently.This is why we built o11y-bench, Grafana Labs' open benchmark for evaluating AI models on observability and SRE tasks. And today, we're excited to share two updates: o11y-bench is now part of the Specialized Intelligence Index from Fireworks, the AI training and inference platform, and we're releasing o11y-bench 1.1, with updates that make grading more grounded, consistent, and reproducible.Bringing o11y-bench to the Specialized Intelligence IndexThe Specialized Intelligence Index brings together practitioner-built benchmarks for comparing how open, closed, and specialized AI models perform on domain-specific work, from healthcare and finance to cybersecurity and software engineering. It helps teams identify the best models for their workloads, understand where specialization adds value, and evaluate tradeoffs between quality, cost, and speed.With o11y-bench now part of the index, SRE, platform engineering, and observability teams can explore how AI models perform on real observability workflows—from querying metrics, logs, and traces to investigating incidents and managing Grafana dashboards—alongside benchmarks for other specialized domains and use cases.Run the benchmark with Fireworks inference o11y-bench also now supports Fireworks as an inference provider in its default LiteLLM-backed agent. This means teams can evaluate both serverless models and models deployed within their own Fireworks accounts, using the same reproducible workflow available for other providers.The integration handles Fireworks credentials, deployment names, and reasoning settings so benchmark runs are configured consistently. This makes it easier to reproduce results from the index or evaluate Fireworks-hosted models against your own requirements. How o11y-bench evaluates models on real observability tasks Observability deserves a place in model evaluation. During an incident, the hard part is rarely generating valid PromQL, LogQL, or TraceQL code. An engineer, or an agent, has to identify the relevant signal, use the right time range, connect evidence across telemetry types, distinguish a symptom from a cause, and sometimes modify persistent state without breaking something another engineer depends on.o11y-bench evaluates those capabilities and more in a running Grafana stack. Agents use the Grafana MCP server to work with synthetic but realistic telemetry and complete 64 tasks across six areas:Prometheus and PromQLLoki and LogQLTempo and TraceQLMulti-step incident investigationsGrafana API workflowsDashboard creation, editing, and repairThe tasks are focused enough to grade, but still reflect real challenges engineers face in day-to-day observability workflows. For example, a query can be syntactically correct while selecting the wrong series, and a dashboard can still render even though its variables, data source, or saved query are wrong.For this reason, o11y-bench starts with outcomes. It compares an agent’s claims with facts read from the same environment, and inspects the state the agent leaves behind. In other words, a convincing answer isn't enough; the results need to back it up. Why consistency matters Each o11y-bench task is run three times. The benchmark measures not just whether a model can solve a task once, but how consistently it performs that task across repeated attempts.That consistency is especially important for observability. A model that reaches the right answer one time might follow a false lead or report an unsupported value the next. During an incident, that inconsistency can cost time and make it harder for teams to trust the results.o11y-bench prioritizes Pass^3, the average benchmark score across three runs, while also reporting Pass@3, which captures whether the model succeeded at least once. Looking at both helps separate occasional wins from repeatable performance.Strengthening the benchmark: what’s new in o11y-bench 1.1Alongside o11y-bench's inclusion in the Specialized Intelligence Index, we’re releasing o11y-bench 1.1, which makes grading more outcome-based, reproducible, and resistant to answers that sound right without being grounded in the environment. The improvements fall into three areas:Grounded outcomes: Rather than rewarding a particular approach or phrasing, o11y-bench checks the outcome: whether the model’s claims match the facts, its saved changes are correct, and its behavior meets the task’s requirements. Reported numbers are checked against reference values, and cited traces are read back from Tempo to verify that they support the agent’s claims.Deterministic grading: Dashboard edits are evaluated using before-and-after diffs of saved state. If a ground-truth query is empty or fails, the result is treated as a grading error rather than being allowed to influence pass rates.Reproducible, calibrated evaluation: Saved facts let results be regraded without rerunning the agent, and scenarios remain consistent over time. A no-tools control failed all 64 tasks, showing that plausible answers alone cannot pass. Because o11y-bench 1.1 uses updated grading and task calibration, its results are not directly comparable with 1.0. Version 1.1 establishes a new baseline for future comparisons. Open benchmarks make better benchmarkso11y-bench’s tasks, environments, grading logic, and results are all open source. That means anyone can examine how the benchmark works, reproduce its results, and help identify areas for improvement.Adding o11y-bench to the Specialized Intelligence Index extends that work to a broader model-evaluation effort. We’re excited to see observability represented alongside other specialized domains, and to give engineering teams more evidence for evaluating the models they use in their workflows.We also expect the benchmark to keep evolving. New models, agent harnesses, observability tools, and failure modes will expose gaps and create opportunities to make the evaluation stronger. As always, we welcome feedback and contributions from the community as part of that process.To get started:Compare models: Explore the o11y-bench results in Fireworks’ Specialized Intelligence Index.Understand the benchmark: Review the tasks, categories, and detailed results at o11ybench.ai.Run it or contribute: Visit the o11y-bench repository on GitHub.

title: Fragments: October 28
description:
Andrej Karpathy sees a widening gap in how people see LLM capabilities.


  The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.


Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at  Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly. It was full of those who are experiencing that vertigo of LLM capabilities, so it felt very much like being in a bubble of those on the bleeding edge. While it’s worth remembering that that’s not a typical view of what’s happening, it’s good to see what those explorers are experiencing. (As I talk about this, I’m applying the Chatham House rule, if anyone wants attribution, let me know.)

A couple of folks talked about doing immersion courses to help teach developers how to do agentic engineering. The idea is to get people out of their usual work environment, and spend one or two weeks with experienced coaches, learning how to use these tools well. Such things remind me very much of the Extreme Programming immersion classes I was involved with at the turn of the century. As with that, the experience of building something is important to understand such a new style of work.

Unsurprisingly the coaches observed that the biggest impact wasn’t technical, but emotional. New tools are just new tools, but these tools change basic assumptions of what it means to be a software developer, which for many people challenges their identity. One coach said how his main job was to take such people out for a walk to a coffee shop, so they could process what’s happening. (This reminds me of a participant of the Extreme Programming immersion who was so horrified by the use of a non-locking version-control system (CVS) that he walked out of the class on the first day.)

 ❄                ❄

I’m wary of talking about themes to an event where I attend less than one-tenth of the sessions, but a topic I kept coming across was how large enterprises were embracing this technology - or rather not. One participant used a lovely metaphor: corporations have acquired a Swiss-army knife, but are only using the toothpick. I see plenty of decent reasons for this: it’s one thing for a startup or individual to use a hot technology, but there’s a big difference between a website going down and your factories grinding to a halt. Big organizations involve workflows involving lots of people that have built up over many years - they don’t change easily. Security concerns abound, the lethal trifecta still lurks.

In particular good use of AI in enterprises relies on good data, and many such organizations don’t have their data in a decent shape. The path to getting agent-ready data isn’t trivial and it’s hard to see how we can get the knife and saw out until enterprises are much further down that path. One thing that struck me is that there was little conversation about this at Foocamp - a sign of its visibility among the people there.

 ❄                ❄

I very much enjoyed Foocamp, but events like this are always a mix of excitement and dread. I knew very few of the people there, so it was a great opportunity to get out of my own social bubble. But I also find it nearly impossible to walk up to people I don’t know (or know slightly) and impose my company on them. The great thing about unconferences is that the nature of the sessions make it plausible for someone like me to engage in conversation during them, and begin some tentative links. Also I thank the many folks there who were friendly to me as I casually walked around trying to hide how much I was panicking.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Laurie Voss says today is 1997


  On Saturday, Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok published No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector. It’s short and it’s blunt: outside of 7 major tech companies, there is no data yet to support a productivity gain that justifies all the money pouring into tech.

  My position is that he’s half right: are valuations too high? Absolutely. We’re in a bubble, and it’s absolutely going to pop. But does that mean investing in AI is a waste of money? Absolutely not, and using this early data to try and decide that question would be like trying to decide in 1997 whether the Internet was going to pay off. The data just isn’t there yet, because these things take time.


I’m not as sure as he is that we can peg today to 1997 rather than 1999, but I agree that this boom bears a lot of resemblance to the dotcom boom (although I think this one is bigger). While many dotcom companies crashed (I always think of pets.com and webvan) he’s right to point out that anyone who invested in Amazon in 1997 did very well. Where might those good investments be this time?


  if you can build something that proves you got the answer, AI can get the answer much faster than you can, and there are real productivity gains to be had doing that generally.


As we think about this, remember that investment isn’t just buying shares, but also where we choose to invest that precious resource of our time and energy.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Adam Tornhill asks Were All Those Years of Coding Wasted?


  For me, agentic coding is enjoyable because it lets me take on larger parts of a problem than I would have been able to master manually. Infrastructure updates are no longer a blocker. And I don’t need to spend time learning about a build system I never cared about.

  My personal goal is to get better at working with higher-level abstractions, and accept that writing code is likely to be a dying skill. My bet on the future is that our problem solving skills, logical mindset, and understanding of systems will be at least as rewarding.

  In the end, we only need to challenge our identity if we mistake programming for writing code. AI finally allows us to separate the two. And that’s where all those years of experience transfer the best: knowing not only what to build but how to build it well.


 ❄                ❄

Tim Bray looks at this from another direction


  For me (and I’m not alone), the biggest issue isn’t what GenAI can and can’t do, it’s the ethical and economic discomforts. This technology is being peddled by terrible people who are rich and whose goal is to get richer. It’s bought and deployed by terrible people who want to slash their payrolls by throwing thought workers onto the street. It facilitates the oncoming climate catastrophe and devalues human creative effort.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Annie Vella observes that the change we’re seeing in software development follows a way of thinking about automation that goes back to the 1960’s as the distinction between  direct and supervisory control.


  The main difference between direct and supervisory control is that in the latter, there’s a computer that closes the loop instead of a human operator. Before AI, writing software was much more like direct control - we closed the loop ourselves. We interpreted requirements, made changes to the code, received feedback and acted on it, over and over. Now, coding agents can increasingly close that loop themselves - writing code, running tests and fixing their own mistakes - while we move towards supervisory control: telling the agent what we want, keeping an eye on how it’s going and taking over when we need to.


She outlines various ideas that this intellectual thread developed. The five-level model developed by Endsley and Kiris seems apposite:


  
    
      Level
      Human
      System
      In AI-assisted software development
    
  
  
    
      1. None
      Decide, act
      -
      No AI assistance
    
    
      2. Decision support
      Decide, act
      Suggest
      The early days of AI coding assistants’ autocomplete
    
    
      3. Consensual AI
      Concur
      Decide, act
      AI coding agents where you must approve the actions they take
    
    
      4. Monitored AI
      Veto
      Decide, act
      Auto-mode, with the ability to veto the coding agent’s actions
    
    
      5. Full automation
      -
      Decide, act
      Full auto-mode, such as might be used in a dark software factory
    
  


Vella cautions that this comes with an important caveat:


  There is one notable difference between the automation described by this prior research and the type of automation that AI agents give us. Both sets of levels assume that the computer’s account of what it did is accurate and honest. As we all know by now, what an AI agent says it did and what it actually did may not be the same thing. Still, it’s automation, and it still requires supervision - arguably more, since we can’t simply take its word for it.


Vella’s conclusion from all this is that: “our next step must be to start redesigning the job and the system, in tandem”. I agree with this, and the Foocampers’ immersion courses I mentioned earlier are part of that exercise. The tricky thing is that we don’t yet know what this new job design looks like, but I think Vella is on the right path when she says:


  What if we stopped thinking of the SDLC as a process we follow, and instead started thinking of it as a control system we build and supervise?


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

A while ago I mentioned how much I enjoyed Eric Evans’s keynote at DDD Europe. Now the video is available so those who weren’t in Antwerp can watch it.

He opens by looking at our future, saying that rather than fruitlessly trying to predict it, we should instead explore it with “curiosity, fun, and wonder”. He’s been doing this, digging deeper into the theory and fundamentals that underpin AI.

He goes into detail on his side project: the Domain Language Surveyor. The idea is to be able to examine different repositories, and analyze the vocabulary used inside those repositories to see if they are related bounded contexts. To do this he built a pipeline of tools, illustrating how a useful system blends both computational and inferential components. He then used this pipeline to analyze the vocabulary of some open-source healthcare codebases, to see how their bounded contexts related.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

A topic that regularly comes up when I talk to companies outside the Foocamp world, is the cost of tokens, and the concern about how that cost is going to increase in the future. We’ve been worrying about that at Thoughtworks, and my colleague Andy Nolan describes our token sourcing strategy, which we forecast will reduce our token costs in 2028 from $16-40M  down to $6.8-1M.


  The strategy rents frontier models for the work that needs frontier-level reasoning. It runs open-weight models, on capacity we choose, for the work that carries our IP or runs at a volume where owning the capacity costs less.


The strategy involves looking at each LLM workload, and classifying it on two axes: domain differentiation and security & sovereignty. We then place each workload on a nine cell grid.


  The nine cells run from the cheapest capable API, swapped as prices change, to a fine-tuned open model on our own infrastructure, with full control and full upkeep. For a given workload, the highest score on a given axis determines the right position in the grid. There is no single right place for all workloads. Each organization ends up with its own distribution and mix of workloads across the grid.
